department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: PREDICTING THE POPULAR VOTE FOR UNITED STATES PRESIDENTIAL ELECTIONS: FUNDAMENTAL VARIABLES VERSUS POLITICAL VARIABLES
abstract: Presidential Elections can be forecast using a variation of methods. Statisticians, politicians, and many others attempt to predict elections using a variety of methods and variables. Specifically, there are two prevailing methods of predicting US presidential elections which are explored in this paper: fundamentals based models and political variables based models. The paper highlights the advantages and disadvantages of both types of variables by building two separate models by using the same data set. The model consists of two stages: a bivariate regression stage to weed out variables with less predicting power and a multilinear regression model to put together the remaining variables. Ultimately, the model demonstrates that around 40% and 75% of voting behaviour can be predicted by fundamental variables and political variables respectively.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Efficiency of Chinese College Admission Mechanisms: a Perspective from Matching Theory and Online Learning Algorithms
abstract: Since the new century, the Chinese college admission mechanism has shifted from an Immediate Acceptance (IA) style mechanism to a Deferred Acceptance (DA) style mechanism. Although DA is often regarded as a superior matching mechanism than IA, their social welfare implications are not clear. This paper defines a new property called sensitive-to-top choice, and finds that this class of mechanism generates stable matching in equilibrium. When there is uncertainty regarding the ranking of students, this paper uses no-regret online learning algorithms to model students, and study the equilibrium properties of admission mechanisms in the Chinese context. I find that DA generates slightly higher expected efficiency, while IA exhibits less volatility. A more realistic model of the current Chinese college scheme, the Parallel Acceptance Mechanism (PA) lies between DA and IA in expected efficiency. The volatility of PA lies in the middle of PA and IA when the population size is large.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Twister: Untangling the Effects of the CDBG-DR Grant on Joplin, MO
abstract: On May 22, 2011 an EF-5 tornado hit Joplin, Missouri, causing approximately $3 billion in damage. This paper analyzes the economic impact of the tornado and the Community Development Block Grant – Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) administered by HUD to facilitate recovery. The paper finds little evidence of major lasting economic impact of the disaster or subsequent HUD funding on unemployment or wage rates, despite seeing a temporary rise in homelessness and an increase building permit requests for reconstruction.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Effects of Patent Expiration on Prescription Rates of Different Branded and Generic Drugs
abstract: This paper examines the impact brought upon by the introduction of generic alternatives, after a drug loses its patent exclusivity, on prescription rates of certain branded drugs, their generics and their therapeutic substitutes. The study uses provider level prescription data from Medicare Part D Prescriber Datasets to focus on 10 highly profitable drugs whose patents expired between the years 2014-2017. This research provides evidence that the generic share of prescriptions one year post-patent expiration of a branded drug has continued to increase in the US. Using a regular cross-section regression model, the paper finds that there is no correlation between the change in prescription behavior of physicians and the per capita income of the zip codes in which they practice medicine. Also, the study shows that any potential effects of business stealing from therapeutic substitutes, upon the introduction of a generic version of a leading molecule, are offset by other external factors affecting the entire drug class.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Impact of Unemployment, Income, and Cash Transfer Payments on Suicide: Evidence from the U.S. and Alaska, 1976-2019
abstract: From 2000 to 2018, the U.S. suicide rate rose by 41.7% to 14.8 deaths per 100,000 annually. Could this trend be reversed by providing citizens with a universal basic income? In this paper, I use both state-level data for the entire U.S. and state-level data for Alaska to examine the effects of unemployment, income, and cash transfer payments on suicide over the 1976-2019 period. Using data for the entire U.S., I estimate that a one percentage-point increase in the unemployment rate is predicted to increase the suicide rate by 1.0%. Controlling for unemployment, I find no association between per capita income and suicide. While, using regression analysis of state-level data for Alaska, I find no association between Alaska Permanent Fund dividend (APFD) payments and suicide, I conclude by arguing, with the use of descriptive statistics, that larger APFD payments could potentially improve mental health outcomes for Alaskans with low socioeconomic status.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Effects of the Chicago Public School Socioeconomic Tier System on Minority Enrollment at Top Selective Enrollment High Schools
abstract: Since 2009, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) has employed a race-neutral, socioeconomic tier system to determine admission into its selective enrollment high schools (SEHS). Prior to 2009, CPS employed a race-based affirmative action system where seats at SEHS were determined by racial quotas. Since the change was implemented, the share of White students at the top five SEHS has increased from 32% to 38%, while the share of Black students has declined from 19% to 11%. Asian and Hispanic students as a share of the top five SEHS student body has remained relatively stagnant. First, I will examine if and how the tier system has disproportionately affected minority students. Then, I will propose modifications to the tier system that can be used to rebalance the percentages of minority students.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: An Examination of the Value of Education in China: What are the returns to education in China? Does it make sense for Chinese international students to study in the U.S.?
abstract: Higher education in the United States is on average more costly than any other country, yet despite this, Chinese students, consisting the largest group of international students in the U.S., are at an all time high. Does this trend of Chinese students leaving China to study in the U.S. make sense? This paper attempts to answer this question through evaluating the Mincer returns to education of 2013 China and comparing it with the value of the U.S. among other countries already derived in existing literature. Upon finding a 6.06% returns to education value in 2013 China, we compare it to the U.S. and after considering costs for international students, determined that it was preferable for Chinese students to remain in China for higher education.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Does One Size (Model) Fit All? Effects of Body Size on Clothing Attitudes

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Effect of Having Children on Gender Inequality in the Labor Market: Evidence from the China Family Panel Studies

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: What Are Professional Baseball Teams Paying For: An Analysis of Wins Above Replacement Data For MLB Draftees

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Investigating the Relationship Between Homeownership and Land Use Regulation

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Misallocation, Decentralization, and Growth in China: Empirical Evidence and Theoretical Framework

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: FEELINGS ABOUT BEING SOCIAL ONLINE: A CORRELATIONAL STUDY OF SOCIAL MEDIA USAGE, ANXIETY, SLEEP AND DIGITAL STRESS
abstract: Social media has become increasingly influential in people’s life. Though the existing body of literature on how social media usage (SMU) can affect one’s mental well-being is already extensive, the results are not conclusive. While some argue the usage is detrimental, others argue that people can build effective support networks through social, thus improving mental health outcomes. The current research investigates how problematic SMU is associated with people’s anxiety levels among college students. In addition, the study aims to investigate the roles of sleep quality and digital stress as mediators in the relationship between anxiety and problematic SMU. Last, the study examines how these relationships differ among American and Chinese populations. Both American (N = 77) and Chinese (N =144) college undergraduate students participated in the study. We found that excessive SMU is not a predictor of college students’ anxiety levels through Pearson correlation analysis and logit regression analysis with and without mediation effect. However, addictive SMU is a better predictor and positively correlates with anxiety. In addition, both sleep disturbance and digital stress serve as mediators in the relationship between anxiety and addictive SMU. Additionally, the mediation effect of digital stress is only manifest in the Chinese population, whereas the mediation effect of sleep disturbance is present in both populations. Further research should look into other mediators on the effect of SMU on anxiety to clarify the benefits or detriments of SMU, and how effect of SMU differs in various cultures.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Running on Empty: Examining the Effects of COVID-19 on the Behavior of MLB Umpires
abstract: This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the behavior of MLB umpires, particularly their tendency to favor the home team with incorrect calls, and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on this phenomenon, as we saw empty stadiums in baseball for the first time. I begin by verifying that this umpire home-team bias exists. I then explore the effects of the pandemic, finding that umpire favor decreased as a result of COVID. Next, I analyze the relationship between umpire favor and stadium attendance, using attendance brackets to isolate the observed effect and more precisely determine the reasons for this umpire bias. I conclude with potential directions for future research.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: You Lie, I Leave: Dynamic Cheap Talk under Receiver Commitment
abstract: When can naive agents influence the recommendations of an expert? Consider a dynamic cheap talk game where receivers directly accept recommendations from a privately informed sender. Generically, senders can secure their maximal payoff by directly recommending their most preferred action. However, when receivers can commit to ignore future messages, they can link senders’ incentives across time to induce truthful revelation. I formalize this intuition, explicitly construct an equilibrium, and show all equilibria are behaviorally equivalent. When payoffs are concave supermodular, every equilibrium is summarized by a cutoff statistic: misrepresentation occurs only if the state is sufficiently high. If states are intertemporally correlated, equilibrium are ranked: more informative correlation structures decrease truthfulness. Should senders have reputational concerns, commitment leads to state-contingent interval pooling of types, encouraging truthfulness. Finally, I apply these insights to discuss optimal enforcement of perjury law and communication by a (potentially) corrupt government.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: THE IMMEDIATE AND SUBSEQUENT EFFECTS OF RANKED-CHOICE VOTING ON VOTER TURNOUT
abstract: Ranked-Choice Voting (RCV) is a voting system where voters are tasked to rank the candidates in an election. A candidate wins if they have received over 50% of the first-choice vote. If not, the candidate with the least first-choice votes is eliminated, and thus voters' rankings are accordingly adjusted until a winner emerges. There are contradicting opinions about how this voting system affects voter turnout. This paper highlights the effect of RCV on voter turnout in both state elections and presidential elections in Minnesota. The data shows that RCV tends to increase voter turnout and that the increase is more pronounced in subsequent elections after the implementation of RCV.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Transmission of US Stock Market Shocks: Comparison Across Time, Causes, and Journalistic Certainty
abstract: The global financial market is interconnected, and shocks from the US spread through global markets. Hence, it is crucial to understand the patterns in the transmission of market shocks. This paper aims to compare the spatial dependence among 17 national stock market indices for various categories of market shocks originating from the United States. I use the Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) Model to estimate the effect of the US market shocks on other countries’ national stock markets. I evaluate the difference in transmission and US direct impact by categorizing shocks by time, perceived causes, and journalistic confidence in reporting the causes. I find that spatial dependence increased over time, and policy-induced have shown a higher degree of spatial dependence than non-policy shocks. Further, when journalists are confident in identifying the underlying cause of stock market jumps, spatial dependence and US direct impact increase.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Statelessness in Estonia and Latvia
abstract: This thesis discusses the post-Soviet situation of statelessness in Latvia and Estonia: the context that it exists in, the trends that can be modeled through time series, its relationship to economic factors and amendments through OLS models, and the past literature surrounding it. The paper uses ARIMA models to enable predictions based on 2004-2020 trends in population proportion. The models predict that despite Latvia having a faster stateless dissolution rate, their initial higher proportion in population. The data examined through visualizations and models include sources from 1991 to 2020.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Feasibility of Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems: Simulation Evidence from the California Electricity Market
abstract: Recent technological progress has allowed battery energy storage systems to become a larger part of the US energy infrastructure. The demand for such technologies is expected to increase tremendously in the coming years as renewable technology continues to take up a larger market share of electricity generation. Most engineering life cycle analyses of these BESS and ESS technologies fail to account for the nuances of market conditions. On the other hand, many analyses in the economics literature are far more data-intensive and less computationally tractable. I develop an easy-to-use model for analyzing the impact and feasibility of such storage technologies on an electricity market and test this model using data from up-to-date technological performance analyses and the California electricity market.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: A Study into the Most Optimal Majors at Northwestern: Balancing Academic Life-Satisfaction with Post-Graduate Income
funding: MMSS Michael F. Dacey Research Grant

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Secondhand Becomes First Choice? The Impact of Luxury Consignment Store Openings on Traditional Retailers in the United States, 2018-2021
abstract: Since its emergence in 2014, luxury resale had grown to a size of $36 billion dollars in 2021, comprising both online and brick-and-mortar businesses. Could the emergence of a liquid consignment market diminish the popularity of traditional fashion stores? In this paper, I use foot traffic data from 2018 to 2021 to examine the effect of luxury consignment shop openings on brand name boutiques and department stores in the United States. Applying a difference-in-difference model with controls, I find that the introduction of secondhand fashion has a positive albeit insignificant effect on visits to existing stores that especially holds true for boutiques and stores exposed to a handbag consignment shop opening nearby. The results of the analysis suggest that rather than undermining the status of firsthand stores, resale locations offer additional opportunities to explore luxury items which that can foster brand education and consumers to frequent traditional retailers.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Engineering Correlated Parlays in the NFL with Spread Winners and Point Totals
abstract: As sports betting becomes mainstream in the United States, individuals from all backgrounds and locations have a newfound ability to participate in a marketplace where billions of dollars are won and lost. Joining the efforts of other researchers in search of money-making strategies, I sought to find an inefficiency in the National Football League (NFL) betting market by testing the bookmaker assumption of independence between point totals and game outcomes. I found evidence that bettors have the ability to place correlated parlay bets by wagering on both the spread winner and the point total in matchups where one team is more likely to perform better in either high scoring games or low scoring games than the other. The payout of parlay bets is conditional on the underlying bets being independent and any sort of correlation represents an advantageous opportunity for a bettor. Two logistic regression models were developed, with one being designed to predict whether a team is more likely to win in a high scoring game (over model) and the other being designed to do the same for lower scoring games (under model). These models were trained on NFL games from 2010-2022 and back tested on both in sample and out of sample data using various confidence thresholds to determine bet selection. In sample returns on the over model were strikingly lucrative and consistent across confidence thresholds. The under model had fewer confident predictions which led to a smaller betting sample, however the bets under this strategy were highly profitable and succeeded at a rate far above expectation. Unlike many other strategies in the field, both models also exhibited out of sample profits over a five year sample. These results were impressive, but a larger sample is required for statistical significance. An examination of the model variables revealed that the characteristics which correlate to a team playing well in high-scoring games are a strong passing offense and a weak opposing defense, while the characteristic which correlates to playing well in low-scoring games was primarily the presence of a strong defense.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Does Self-Regulation Predict Relationship Quality? Evaluating the Effects of Cognitive Self-Regulation and Emotion Regulation on Various Social Outcomes
abstract: OBJECTIVE - This study examines how self regulation and emotion regulation impact various social outcomes. HYPOTHESIS - I hypothesize that greater self regulation is associated with more optimal social outcomes (H1), measured by considering self-reports about various aspects of a person’s social life. I also hypothesize that emotion regulation would mediate the association between self regulation and satisfaction of social life (H2). METHODS - Relationships between self regulation, emotion regulation, and numerous social outcomes were explored across three ICPSR datasets using bivariate correlation, simple linear regression, factor analysis, multiple linear regression, and mediation analysis. RESULTS - In study 1, I found that self regulation constructs were significantly associated with self-reported quality of relationships, social integration, and the length of one’s romantic relationship. In study 2, I found that proxies for self regulation, cognitive control and self control, were significantly associated with affectual solidarity shown to family, friends, and partner, frequency of contact with friends, feelings of closeness to others, and trust between self and friends. In study 3, I found that self regulation was significantly associated with lower assessments of the probability of separating from a partner, contact with family and friends, and fewer disagreements with one’s partner. Across all studies, emotion regulation was found to not be consistently statistically significant mediator between self regulation and social outcome. CONCLUSIONS - I found self regulation to be a significant predictor of the quality of one’s relationships and the degree to which one is socially integrated within their community. Findings also indicate that emotion regulation does not have a significant effect on these social outcomes nor does it mediate the relationship betweens self regulations and social outcome.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Impact of Digitalization: What Can Technology Adoption Tell Us about the International Economic Response to the COVID-19 Pandemic?

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Effects of Price Transparency Legislation on Hospital Profitability
abstract: I examine the effects of price transparency legislation on hospital financial performance. By exploiting the exogenous impact of the 2012 Massachusetts Cost Containment Law, I find that price transparency has a negative impact on operating and total margins in the short run. Although the effects are temporary, the magnitude of the impact is sizable enough to make the average hospital unprofitable, which could unintentionally harm healthcare access in rural and disadvantaged communities. I find a clear difference between short and long run effects of the law change, suggesting that hospitals respond to price transparency legislation. These results have implications for legislators when constructing and implementing price transparency rules in the future.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Where is All the Good Food? Michelin Guide Clusters and Neighborhood Characteristics in Chicago
abstract: This thesis aims to develop a model to determine the likelihood of encountering a high quality restaurant in Chicago based on the characteristics of the area surrounding the restaurant. The study employs a data-driven approach, utilizing commercially available data on the characteristics of Chicago’s neighborhoods, data on the kinds of people who live in those neighborhoods and publicly available data on the Michelin Guide. The data is analyzed using logit and ordered logit regression models. The results of the study provide insights into whether high quality restaurants are agglomerated in the city of Chicago and what characteristics they might be agglomerated by. In particular, the study analyzes the Michelin Guide as the premier measure of quality for restaurants.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: How can Social Network Analysis and Mapping be leveraged to inform Chicago STEAM Out of School Time (OST) Policy Decisions?

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Hoops and Higher Education Evaluating how college basketball TV exposure along with a team’s success influences the admissions numbers of universities?
abstract: Given the immense pageantry and tremendous investment that surrounds the world of college sports, it should come as no surprise that the role of college athletics within a larger context of higher education is consistently under intense scrutiny. Regular questions are raised about the utility of college sports in general, asking if there are tangible benefits to transferring funds away from aspects of a university like academics and towards athletics. My thesis seeks to answer this question through the lens of basketball and college admissions. Does college athletic success or playing games on national television and ESPN increase application numbers, decrease acceptance rates, increase admissions yield, or increase the test scores of incoming classes in the future? My analysis finds that the link between basketball success and different admissions statistics is weak. However, I do find that basketball appearances on national television and ESPN are correlated with higher application rates and a higher quality student body, in terms of test scores. I therefore conclude that while basketball success does not have a tangible influence on admissions statistics, investment in basketball programs is still important. Maintaining good standing within a big time conference that has television contracts with popular networks requires investment. Similarly, winning games during a season not only produces excitement around a team, making appearances on television more likely, but winning prolongs the season and increases a university’s chances of playing important postseason games on the biggest networks in the country.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Optimizing Medical Resource Allocation for Mortality Reduction during Pandemic Outbreaks Using Non-Homogenous Markov Chain
abstract: This study proposes a theoretical framework using non-homogeneous Markov chain to simulate the dynamics of a pandemic outbreak and to predict mortality rates under different resource allocation strategies. By categorizing individuals based on infection status and underlying health conditions, the model captures transitions between categories with time-dependent probabilities. We calibrate the model using data from Mexico's pandemic outbreak in 2020 and conduct simulations to derive insights on optimal medical resource allocation. The findings indicate that reserving resources for non-pandemic patients not only balances access to treatment but also reduces overall mortality. Additionally, a flexible reserve system that adapts to the increasing severity of a pandemic yields lower mortality rates than fixed reserve systems, making it a more favorable allocation strategy for policymakers.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: An Indirect Effect of Immigration Trends: Household Labor Supply Shifts and the Labor Outcomes of Educated Women
abstract: The ability to outsource domestic labor is essential for women with high-earning potential. Since immigrants represent a large portion of the workforce in household production and childcare industries, I examine how the concentration of immigrants in a county and the enforcement of the federal immigration policy Secure Communities (SC) impact high-educated women’s labor outcomes. I find that high-educated women in counties with a higher immigrant concentration are more likely to work and earn more income than their peers. In counties where SC is active, high-educated women with young children are less likely to work than those in non-active counties. Further, quantities of submissions and deportations from SC have no influence on the labor outcomes of high-educated women. I conclude that the mere threat of a strict immigration policy is enough to cause sizable immigrant labor supply shocks that negatively influence the availability of domestic services, worsening women’s career opportunities.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: How Market Maker Inventory Affects Option Liquidity
abstract: This paper analyzes how market maker inventory affects liquidity in S&P 500 options. Using vega, gamma, and risk-neutral skew as inventory measures, I find that there is less options liquidity when aggregate inventory across all three risk measures is negative. The relationship is strengthened during times of market turmoil and volatility. In addition, periods of high option expensiveness correspond with flat market maker portfolios. This paper extends other studies that analyze singular inventory risks and the costs associated with hedging and rebalancing market maker portfolios.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Understanding the Satisfaction of Maximizers Across Choice Domains
abstract: As people make endless choices, the psychology behind decision-making continues to be a fascinating subject to study. Much of the current research in economics and the cognitive sciences focuses on the distinction between two types of decision-makers: maximizers and satisficers. The present study seeks to determine what rationales (focusing on regret, social comparison, and exposure to negative outcomes) drives maximizers’ satisfaction or dissatisfaction with their choices. In addition, this study aims to understand how choice complexity affects the behavior of maximizers and satisficers and their subsequent satisfaction with the outcomes of their decisions. 79 first-year students at Northwestern University participated in an online study, answering a set of questions about two different choices. The first choice was actively made during the study and consisted of choosing a poster from a collection. The second choice was retrospective and looked at participants’ decision to attend Northwestern. Overall, maximizers exerted more effort in the decision-making process than satisficers in both choices, confirming previous study results. However, maximization tendency had a significant negative correlation with satisfaction only when analyzing college decisions, suggesting that choice complexity plays a role in whether maximizers experience less satisfaction than satisficers. Overall, regret was the rationale most consistently and significantly associated with lower satisfaction, but there was no significant difference in its effect on maximizer and satisficer satisfaction. Social comparison demonstrated the opposite effect. It was associated almost always with higher satisfaction for both maximizers and satisficers. Finally, exposure to negative outcomes had no consistent effect on satisfaction. Further research may continue to investigate the role of choice complexity in the distinction between maximizers and satisficers as well as the possibility of other key rationales affecting satisfaction.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Addressing Verification Dilemma: Improving Zero-Knowledge Proof for Multiple Verifiers in a Non-Interactive Setting
abstract: This thesis presents a general improvement to multiple verifier non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIMVZK) protocols by converting sigma protocols to strong NIMVZK with fiat-shamir transformation and proposing a consistency check mechanism to detect dishonest verifiers. The security guarantee of this proposed protocol suggests a theoretical improvement to the soundness error of the NIMVZK model. The actual security and efficiency of the proposed model are demonstrated through simulation experiments under different settings. Finally, the thesis concludes by addressing the implications of such improvements in zero-knowledge protocols under the context of social settings, especially in resolving the various verification dilemma in law and business areas.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Breaking Balls and Breaking Laws: Investigating Allegations of Owner Collusion in the 2002-03 MLB Offseason
abstract: In the 2002-03 Major League Baseball offseason, many free agents received unreasonable contract offers that prompted the players’ union to file allegations of collusion against team owners. Although the owners denied guilt, they nevertheless settled the grievances with the players’ union for $12 million. The question of whether collusion actually occurred was never answered, which provides the motivation for this paper. I attempt to support allegations of collusion by testing for shocks to the MLB labor market in 2002-03. Specifically, I use three regression-based models to determine whether salary structure was fundamentally different in the 2002-03 offseason. I only find statistically significant evidence of a labor market shock in one of the three models, which is not enough to support collusion allegations on its own. I conclude by emphasizing the necessity of pairing my quantitative approach with additional qualitative inquiries when searching for the presence of collusion in a labor market.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: COMPARING EFFECTS OF INTERCORPORATE INVESTMENTS AND FINANCIAL SPONSOR INVESTMENTS ON POST-IPO OPERATING PERFORMANCE
abstract: This study investigates the effects of intercorporate investments and financial sponsor investments on operating performance. Through utilizing data from a sample of 377 information technology companies in the United States during the period 2000 – 2022, a fixed effects panel regression was used to quantify the impact of equity stakes of financial sponsors and other companies on return on assets and revenue. The results indicate that both types of investments have positive impacts on operating performance, though there are diminishing returns as companies age since going public.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: SMART: A Flexible Approach to Regression using Spline-based Multivariate Adaptive Regression Trees
abstract: Decision trees, such as the Classification and Regression Tree (CART) algorithm, are widely used for predictive modeling but often suffer from high variance. While ensemble methods like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting have been developed to address this issue, they typically rely on simple models in the leaf nodes, which may not effectively capture complex non-linearities and interactions in the data. In this paper, we propose Spline-based Multivariate Adaptive Regression Trees (SMART), a novel algorithm that combines the strengths of Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) with decision trees. SMART handles datasets exhibiting both smooth non-linearities and piecewise changes in the functional form by creating multivariate spline-based functions in the leaf nodes, while requiring minimal hyperparameter tuning for increased user-friendliness and speed. Our approach consists of three main phases: a forward pass based on the MARS algorithm which does feature selection and identifies useful variable interactions, a tree split phase that recursively partitions the data using cross-validation, and a pruning pass that simplifies the model at each leaf node. The algorithm requires little hyperparemeter tuning making it more user-friendly and faster. We describe a computationally efficient and numerically stable fitting algorithm using QR decomposition to find the best-split values. Experimental results on various simulated datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared to popular alternatives such as Random Forests, MARS, XGBoost, and Local Linear Forests. We provide an open-source implementation of the algorithm to facilitate its adoption and further research in this area.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Optimal Electric Bus Charging Station Placement within a Public Network: A COTA Case Study
abstract: The ongoing global green energy transition has created momentous shifts in all industries. One such sector poised for rapid change in the coming years is public bus networks. Many cities have issued pledges to transition fleets to zero-emission vehicles like battery electric buses. The logistics behind this change involve many considerations, including impending infrastructure investments. This paper explores methods to determine optimal locations for on-route electric bus pantograph charging stations within a public network, and applies these methods to the Central Ohio Transit Authority (COTA) network. The model developed is a mixed integer linear programming model. Ultimately, the preliminary findings from this paper detail the locations of an assumption-dependent 9 to 23 charging stations that satisfy network constraints.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Impact of Long-Term Lockdown to Adolescents in China During COVID-19
abstract: COVID-19 has cause challenges to everyone. In China, COVID had led to three years of lockdown and quarantine. Throughout the prolonged process, we believe that adolescents have been impacted the most: disrupted schedules, virtual learning, lack of physical activity, and the absence of social connectedness. In this study, we aim to examine the correlation between quarantine and adolescents’ stress level and the potential protective effect of physical activity and social network. We hypothesize that (1) there is a positive correlation between the lockdown and perceived stress level from the sample. (2) there is a positive correlation between the length of lockdown and perceived stress level. (3) there is a negative correlation between the frequency of physical activity and perceived stress; (4) similarly, there is a negative correlation between the frequency of social connection and perceived stress. In the study, 230 participants of 13-20 years old with average age of 18.03 were asked to complete a survey of Perceived Stress Scale(PSS-10), the Physical Activity Questionnaire for Adolescents (PAQ-A), and Lubben Social Network Scale – 6 (LSNS-6). Respectively, the scales measure the variables of our interest. Based on analyses, the first two hypotheses are supported based on the test statistics. Data show that physical activity is only protective against stress for people who are physically more active than average in regular time, and the data does not support the protective function of social connectedness. The result can bring a different perspective to quarantine and ways to cope with the stress under COVID-like crisis.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Bank Runs, Insolvency, and Competition with Heterogeneous Depositors
abstract: The existing bank run literature on bank run frequently uses homogeneous depositors as a simplifying assumption. This practice is at odds with recent examples of runs, where heterogeneous characteristics of depositors have played a major role in precipitating bank failures. In this thesis, I develop three related models which incorporate depositor homogeneity, generating results about inter-bank competition, bank solvency, and run dynamics. The competition model particularly demonstrates how banks competing incentives for solvency and offering higher yields than competitors interacts with depositor homogeneity, driving excessively risky behavior. Other models in the paper show various tools banks can use to prevent runs by tailoring deposit contracts to relative depositor sizes.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Housing Market Effects of the Chicago Affordable Requirements Ordinance
abstract: Introduced in 2007 and revised in 2015 and 2021, the Chicago Affordable Requirements Ordinance is an inclusionary zoning policy that aims to reduce segregation and gentrification within the city. Existing research on the effects of inclusionary zoning is limited and inconclusive, but the economic theory suggests that such policies may have adverse effects on housing markets. Utilizing two-way fixed effects in a difference-in-differences and event study framework, I contribute to the literature by investigating the effects of inclusionary zoning in the context of the Chicago Affordable Requirements Ordinance.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: What Does Moderate Mean? Using Operational Ideology and Atypical Voting Behavior to Predict Moderate Ideological Identification
abstract: In recent years, moderate voters have often been described as the key to electoral politics in the United States. While moderates have gained substantial mainstream attention, there remains considerable academic debate as to what moderate ideological identification means and whether self-proclaimed moderates truly embody a distinct political ideology. I use Cooperative Election Study (CES) data from the 2008-2020 U.S. presidential election cycles to analyze the roles of operational ideology and atypical voting behaviors in moderate ideological identification. I find statistically significant results, indicating that moderate ideological identification is based on issue area preferences, however, influenced by measurable psychological mechanisms resulting in symbolic ideology inconsistent with operational ideology. This research has important implications for understanding and appealing to an influential yet enigmatic group in American politics.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Extent to Which Parasocial Relationships from Social Media Influence the Self-Esteem and Overall Mental Health of College Students
abstract: This study aims to examine how parasocial relationships from social media impact self-esteem in college students. Parasocial relationships (PSRs) are one-sided relationships developed by audience members in their encounters with figures of the mass media, such as celebrities or social media influencers. The study mainly focuses on measuring the strength of PSRs and looking at their impact. It also looks at the difference between PSRs from visual versus non-visual social media platforms. We collected our data by conducting a survey of college students across the US that asks them about their specific parasocial relationships on various platforms, as well as their global and appearance-based self-esteem. The analysis covered how self-esteem was predicted by the different variables used to capture information about the participants’ PSRs. The main findings were that stronger PSRs led to increased self-esteem on Instagram. Also, the tendency to compare oneself to the subject of a PSR is associated with lowered self-esteem. Finally, the strength of one’s PSR is positively associated with greater desire for reciprocation and tendency towards comparison within a parasocial relationship.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: How does creativity affect moment-by-moment happiness, life satisfaction, and income for college seniors and graduates?

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Impact of Recreational Marijuana Law on the Labor Markets
abstract: This study examines the impact of recreational marijuana legalization (RML) on the labor markets, specifically focusing on unemployment rates and median household income across California, Illinois, and Massachusetts. Utilizing county-level data and employing a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach, the analysis integrates advanced statistical methods to address the dynamic and staggered nature of marijuana policy implementation. The study leverages several estimators, including the Callaway and Sant'Anna’s and Borusyak's methods, to refine the understanding of RML's effects. Results indicate a complex relationship where both unemployment rates show increases in some regions following legalization whereas the income level remains ambiguous. This paper contributes to the discourse on marijuana legalization by elucidating its nuanced economic implications and underscores the need for careful policy consideration to harness potential benefits while minimizing negative impacts on the labor market.

title: Using Machine Learning to Address Adverse Selection in Market Making

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Investigating the Predictors of Real Estate Price Changes in Chicago from 2013 to 2022
abstract: In this paper, I investigate potential drivers of real estate price changes in standard homes in the 35th to 65th percentile of values in Chicago zip codes from 2013 to 2022. Using data primarily from the American Community Survey, I find that the 2013 Price and per-capita income in a zip code result in lower price growth. I hypothesize that this effect could be caused by a maximum price threshold for middle-class home buyers. These results can better inform individuals hoping to evaluate the potential of a real estate investment, as well as Chicago legislators trying to understand disparities between real estate wealth in different areas of the city.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Leveraging Multi-Agent Signals to Improve Decision-Making under Strategic Data Manipulation
abstract: This paper investigates strategic communication, where agents manipulate information to achieve better outcomes from decision-makers. Existing literature suggests that the heterogeneity in agents’ manipulative abilities or stakes makes it optimal for a decision-maker to commit to an ex-post suboptimal policy that agents will respond to. This paper demonstrates that, even if commitment is difficult, a decision-maker can improve the accuracy of evaluating an agent’s quality by incorporating related information from another agent. Reducing sensitivity to the original agent’s manipulated information enhances data informativeness regarding the agent’s quality of interest and partially offsets the drawbacks of non-commitment.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: DQN WITH ACTION EMBEDDINGS FOR MULTIPLAYER CATAN
abstract: This paper explores the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to the strategic board game of Catan. Catan poses several unique challenges to reinforcement learning algorithms with its need for long term planning and stochastic features. Furthermore, this paper considers the three player version of the game which introduces trading leading to a dramatic increase in the number of available moves to the agent. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a modified Deep Q-Network (DQN) that incorporates action embeddings, designed to enhance the ability of the agent to effectively learn and make decisions in the multi-agent environment. We demonstrate this method’s superior performance through both its winrate and decision making in specific game scenarios against traditional DRL algorithms such as traditional DQN and Proximal Policy Optimization in three different environments of varying complexity. We further explore how human knowledge about the hierarchical structure of moves in the game can be incorporated into these embeddings to further improve learning.

title: The Franchise Tag in NFL Contract Nego2a2ons How can we redesign the NFL’s franchise tag to reduce a player’s incen9ve to holdout?

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: THE INCREASING INTENSITY & DURATION OF HARMFUL ALGAE BLOOMS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY ON GLOBAL WARMING AND THE EFFECTS ON TOURISM AND HUMAN MIGRATION IN FLORIDA
abstract: This paper explores the impact of the 2018 Karenia brevis algae bloom in Florida on both tourism and on permanent migration of residents. This paper exploits the exogeneity of this prolonged, persistent, and mild natural disaster by examining zip-code level yearly population counts and county-level monthly data on airline passenger arrivals and tourist development tax. This paper contributes to the ongoing research on the economic impact of a harmful algae bloom (“HAB”) through looking at a more permanent impact: net-migration in impacted areas and by studying two different metrics – airline arrivals and bed tax – metrics that act to directly capture tourism/travel demand and which previous studies have yet to study. This paper concludes that in general, net-migration to Florida is not impacted by the presence of HABs. Further, the study finds that HABs only begin to impact hotel and lodging demand at high concentrations and that there is substantial variation by region. Lastly, the study finds that HABs do not impact airline arrivals. Overall, this paper illustrates how this slow-onset, non-dramatic, but persistent, natural disaster impacts individual’s choices to visit a beach, but does not yet impact their choices to permanently move. The study also highlights the need to collect more granular, detailed population data to better understand the impact of natural disaster on population migration within the United States.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: From Collaboration to Chart-topping Network Analysis and Machine Learning in Music Popularity Prediction
abstract: This research seeks to harness the power of machine learning to predict music popularity with the use of songs’ acoustic features and artist information. The results aim to aid musicians in finding prosperity within the music industry and provide guidance in song creation. With song data collected from Spotify and a network formed on artist collaborations, this study assesses the impact of specific features and partnerships on musical success. A variety of modeling techniques are employed including regularized linear regression models, tree-based models, a K-Nearest Neighbors model, and an ensemble model combining these. The adaptive boost model proved to be the most successful in predictive performance, and it identified key predictive features including artist followers, danceability, energy, liveliness, and speechiness. Although not in the top five most important features, network size also played an influential role in predicting musical success, which revealed the underlying influence of an artist’s network on their song’s popularity. The implications of this research contributes to the understanding of song popularity predictors and the potential application of machine learning within the industry going forward. Furthermore, this novel approach in considering collaborations may be extended to other creative fields in predicting the success of different forms of media.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: THE SPATIAL VARIATION OF THE CRIME-TEMPERATURE RELATIONSHIP ACROSS CHICAGO POLICE DISTRICTS
abstract: There is a substantial body of research studying the relationship between crime and temperature, but there is limited research on the spatial variation of that relationship within cities. In this study, I examine the spatial variation of the impact of temperature on crime across the twenty-two police districts of the city of Chicago. I assume that there is no spatial variation in temperature across Chicago and assess whether certain districts experience significantly different percentage changes in crime from a change in daily temperature. My analysis finds that while an increase in daily temperature leads to increased crime levels for all districts, the magnitude of the percentage increase has significant variation across the districts. The districts in the northwest parts of the city experience a smaller percentage increase in crime with an increase in temperature, whereas the districts near the lake and the center of the city experience a larger increase in crime. District 19, which encompasses much of the Lakeview, Northcenter, and Uptown neighborhoods, has the greatest relationship between temperature and crime levels. The districts that experience a larger percentage increase in crime likely see increased daily migration on hotter days. This would lead to an increase in both likely offenders and suitable targets, which would cause higher levels of crime in line with the routine activities theory.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Neighborhood-Level Variation in Residents’ Self-Reported Socioeconomic Status in Seoul, South Korea
abstract: The contemporary urban landscape of Seoul, the capital city of South Korea, presents a complex tableau of social stratification, particularly seen by disparate economic outcomes between regions and neighborhoods within the city. This thesis uses Multilevel Linear Modeling to examine the layers of individual perceptions of socioeconomic status (SES) in terms of individual- and neighborhood-level socioeconomic disparities and their interactions. The two-level analysis includes individual level measures of household income, education, tenure type, and housing type; and neighborhood level measures of median household income, housing type and tenure type compositions, percentage of homeowners, percentage of social welfare beneficiaries, and higher education advancement rates. I control for individual gender, age, and marital status. I find that while around 2.5% of the total variance in subjective SES is directly attributable to differences between neighborhoods and the rest to differences within neighborhoods, there are meaningful interactions between individual and neighborhood factors specifically relating to household income and education that have a statistically significant impact on the self-reported SES in Seoul.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Does Participation in School Sports Affect Marijuana Use? Impact of School Sports Participation on Adolescent Marijuana Use: A Decade-Long Analysis
abstract: Introduction: This study investigates the relationship between school sports participation and marijuana use among American adolescents, focusing on changes since 2013 and differences by grade and gender. Review of Literature: Previous research on this topic has yielded mixed findings, with some studies suggesting a positive relationship between sports participation and marijuana use, while others have found no significant association. No previous study has looked at the relationship year-by-year and looked at differences by grade and gender. Methods: The study uses data from the Monitoring the Future study, a large-scale survey of American adolescents, to examine the relationship between sports participation and marijuana use. Binary logistic regression models are used to analyze the data, controlling for demographic variables and other school activities. Results: The findings reveal that overall marijuana use in adolescents declined from 2013-2022, with the largest decrease occurring from 2020 to 2021.. Meanwhile, marijuana use is higher among students that participate in school sports for all grades and genders. The change in this relationship, however, varies by group. Conclusion: The study's results suggest that sports participation increases marijuana use among adolescents. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions and further research to better understand these dynamics and inform strategies for promoting healthy behaviors among adolescents.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Equity Market Reactions to Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
abstract: This paper examines the stock market reactions to the adoption of the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which affects both EU and non-EU firms with significant EU presence. We explore the implications of regulations on firms from five non-EU countries and regions - Canada, China, Japan, Hong Kong, United States - using difference-in-differences estimation with EU firms as control group. We posit and find that (i) an overall significant negative market reaction; (ii) a less negative reaction for firms with higher pre-directive ESG disclosure levels; and (iii) a less negative response for firms with lower pre-directive carbon emissions. This study contributes to the existing literature by providing novel evidence on the cross-border impact of EU regulations on non-EU markets, examining the role of firms’ pre-directive ESG practices in shaping market responses, and offering a comprehensive assessment of market reactions across multiple stages of the regulatory process.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Redesigning the Filibuster for More Effective Lawmaking in a Polarized Senate
abstract: In today’s hyper-partisan political environment, it is a common complaint that Congress is broken. This is especially true for the Senate, where the filibuster and cloture rule have created a de facto requirement for a 60-vote supermajority to pass almost any legislation, sparking widespread calls from activists and senators alike to reform or even abolish the filibuster. In this paper, I predict the effects of different proposals for the filibuster and cloture rule on a set of “legislative goods,” including productivity, bipartisanship, and policy stability. I test the effects of three different filibuster rule proposals on these legislative goods. To predict the effects of these rule changes, I extend Wawro and Schickler’s expected-utility model of legislative entrepreneurship under cloture by considering the costs faced by bill proponents and obstructionists alike. Using this model, which excels at explaining the evolution of past filibuster fights, I predict the outcomes of legislative battles under different filibuster rules. The results will inform activists and senators in future debates over filibuster reform — which will inevitably return the next time a popular bill is stymied by the Senate’s supermajoritarian rules.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Evaluating Downstream Healthcare Utilization: A Comparative Analysis of Virtual and In-Person Urgent Care Use Among Medicaid Enrollees
abstract: Motivations: Each year, there is substantial waste in healthcare spending and utilization. Some of this misuse can be attributed to costly in-person care episodes initiated at the ED that could have been handled in a more cost-effective manner, which is particularly common amongst the Medicaid-enrolled population. Due to the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, telemedicine experienced a significant increase in usage by serving as a viable potential alternative to in-person care. However, telehealth’s impact on healthcare spending is not clear and requires careful review. On the one hand, virtual care is – per visit – less expensive than either an in-person UCC or ED visit. Virtual care could increase costs if 1) there is a higher likelihood of follow-up visits if virtual doctors deliver care insufficient to resolve the condition or end up sending patients to in-person care anyway, and 2) it enables patients to seek care they would otherwise would not have, thereby creating new utilization. This study is the first to examine the impact of telehealth on downstream utilization in the Medicaid population specifically. Data: The investigation of subsequent visits in telehealth-initiated episodes involved using claims data from Northwestern Medicine. The sample consisted of 6,370 episodes beginning with either an index in-person (n = 6,007) or telehealth (n = 363) visit with inclusion criteria that patients must be Medicaid-enrollees, above 18 years of age, and experiencing one of a select group of conditions. Methods: The primary outcomes of interest were the likelihood that an index visit type would result in subsequent utilization within a given period, in addition to the number of downstream visits. To run the analysis, logit and Poisson regressions were run on the sample using index visit modality (telehealth or in-person urgent care), age, gender, race/ethnicity, and comorbidities as covariates. Results: Relative to in-person index visits, telehealth is shown to decrease the likelihood of a follow-up visit by 39% (p < 0.01) and result in 0.42 (p < 0.01) less visits on average within a 1-day period. Sensitivity analyses were also used to determine the responsiveness of the model to the length of the follow-up window and inclusion of COVID tests in the sample, both of which produced similar results. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that telehealth does not have an additive effect on healthcare utilization and can potentially optimize Medicaid resources and spending by serving as a more cost-effective and efficient alternative to in-person urgent care.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Strategic Beliefs: A Game Theoretic Approach to Religious and Political Dynamics in Kerala
abstract: This paper explores political motivations and voter behavior across the religious spectrum in Kerala. Through the use of a game theoretical analysis, this paper identifies the ideal political strategy for politicians from differing religious groups and motivations and analyzes the ideal voter behavior as a function of candidate behavior. Using a signaling model, the results of this analysis indicate that there is a difference in the way Hindus, Muslims, and Christians in Kerala vote based on the political motivations of candidates, with the most influential variable being the proportion of each religious group that prioritizes religion in politics.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Next Stop: Gentrification? Investigating the Bay Area Rapid Transit’s Role in Neighborhood Change
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) stations and gentrification in the San Francisco Bay Area using spatial autoregressive lag models. Contrary to the transit-induced gentrification hypothesis, the findings suggest that BART stations do not significantly influence the white population, Asian population, educational attainment, income, or poverty rates in surrounding neighborhoods. The paper advocates for a shift towards a complex systems thinking framework to better understand transit-induced gentrification, emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary approaches that incorporate qualitative evidence and consider power dynamics, equity, and access. Future research directions include applying similar models to other heavy rail transit systems and integrating qualitative methods to provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between transit and gentrification. Overall, this study contributes to ongoing discussions on transit-oriented development and underscores the importance of fostering equitable and sustainable communities through continued research and critical analysis.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: The Impact of Interest Rate Fluctuations on Cryptocurrency Investment Optimization
abstract: The cryptocurrency asset class has experienced increased institutional adoption in the past decade as an investment option. The literature on this subject primarily analyzes the effect of cryptocurrency inclusion in portfolio performance in the context of Modern Portfolio Theory. This thesis aims to extend the existing literature by performing an econometric analysis to determine the effect of interest rates on the optimal allocation of cryptocurrency in various portfolio optimization frameworks. Similar analyses have been performed on alternative assets like real estate as detailed in the literature review. Our analysis considers a diversified portfolio consisting of seven assets and broad indices. We begin by performing the following time-varying optimizations: mean-variance, standard-deviation risk-parity, equal weights, and minimum variance. The time-varying aspect refers to the fact that optimal weights, based on running means, variances, and correlations of the assets, are re-calculated on a running basis after each time period or day. Having determined these optimal weights, the hypothetical portfolio returns can be constructed and regressed on the weight given to Bitcoin (the chosen cryptocurrency asset) in each period. The regression incorporates an interaction term between cryptocurrency weight and interest rate indicators to capture the nuanced impact of rate changes on the risk-adjusted returns associated with varying levels of crypto allocations, accounting for factors such as market volatility and inflation. To resolve the simultaneity and endogeneity issues, we instrument cryptocurrency weight with Bitcoin trading volume, and perform two-stage least squares. Based on the results, we find the risk-parity optimization results suggest a more pronounced diversification benefit of cryptocurrencies during high interest rate environments. This contrasts with the mean-variance optimization results, which show a weaker and less statistically significant relationship.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: Modeling Future Electoral Success with Large Lead Time Using Prior Electoral Success
abstract: This thesis implements an Elo model, commonly seen in chess, to accurately predict elections with a high lead time. Additionally, comparisons to other prediction methods s are made by applying measures of candidate quality obtained from Elo model to national elections. The modified Elo model obtains an out of sample accuracy near the level of prior published models while allowing for a lengthy lead time. Due to data constraints, modeling occurs by looking at data from 1967 – 2010.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: EFFECT OF REMOTE WORK ON LARGE SCALE CITY POPULATIONS IN THE UNITED STATES
abstract: This thesis serves to predict and quantify how work from home effects large scale city populations in the United States. It consists of an introduction and background, in which the rapid technological advancement of today’s world provides motivation for studying the population patterns of large cities in the United States, which are often considered hubs for industries that are becoming increasingly virtual. The thesis will then review some previous literature written surrounding the topic, with a high detail of focus on Jonathan I. Dingel and Brent Neiman’s ”How Many Jobs Can Be Done at Home?” written in 2020. Further analysis of their O*NET-derived baseline scores will be conducted to use for regression analysis on two-digit Standard Occupatioinal Classification (SOC) industries for the fifteen largest Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) in the United States in conjunction with other notable variables such as income level. The analysis has been conducted through the use of Stata coding software and excel coding in some cases. Ultimately, statistical significance was not obtained for many of the industries; however, information regarding the analysis techniques and findings regarding work-from-home capabilities for each industry by MSA still hold importance in the field for future implications regarding the fast-paced digitalization of the United States and the world.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: How Did the Pitch Clock Affect Pitcher Performance? An Application of Econometric Principles
abstract: MLB’s implementation of a pitch clock at the start of the 2023 season represented a massive change to America’s pastime. While controversial for a number of reasons, the pitch clock was unquestionably effective at speeding the game up by reducing the amount of time in between pitches. One of the main issues experts raised with the pitch clock was the potential for injuries for pitchers due to increased fatigue. Fatigue, however, can also lead to reduced pitcher performance. This research aims to determine if the institution of the pitch clock led to changes in the relationship between pitch performance and fatigue on a season-long, game-long, and pitch-by-pitch basis. In this paper I use linear regression with pitcher fixed effects to quantify the effect of the pitch clock on pitch velocity and spin rate of each pitch type. I investigate how the relationship between pitch tempo (the time between pitches) and the target variables changed between the 2022 and 2023 seasons, finding evidence that rest became much more valuable to velocity but not spin rate with the implementation of the pitch clock. I use a second pitcher fixed effects model to model how the relationship between in-game pitch count and the target variables changed between the 2022 and 2023 seasons. While the model shows that the relationships between pitch count and both velocity and spin rate generally became more negative in 2023, it is unclear how much of that change can be attributed to the pitch clock and fatigue directly.

department: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
title: “These Things Exist, Back to Talking About Hetero Relationships”: The Content, Style, and Organization of Gender and Sexual Identity in High-School Health Education
abstract: Queer students tend to experience their school-based health education as inadequate and inapplicable to them, but little research has rigorously studied health education that explicitly acknowledges their existence. This study explores the relationship between content, language, and organization of ideas in New Jersey health curricula to identify patterns across the state. Qualitative, semi-structured interviews were conducted with queer alums (n = 19) and health educators (n = 3) of New Jersey high schools, and preliminary findings were thoroughly tested through mixed-methods coding, content analysis, and topic modeling of curricular documents from New Jersey high schools (n = 91). Both methods support that health education tends to be centered on the needs and experiences of cis, straight students and rely on normative frameworks. This study supplements prior literature and informs advocacy goals by extensively describing a diversity of queer-inclusive curricula and recognizing a trend of explicitly queer-inclusive health education that fails to integrate the experiences and perspectives of queer people holistically within the curriculum.
